claims.text: 111,529 hire events and 111,361 separation events across the period.
claims.source: Census QWI seasonally adjusted, NAICS 326, PIC-12 counties summed
claims.assert: sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) == 111529 and sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) == 111361
claims.actual: (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']), sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']))
claims.falsified_if: QWI re-benchmarks, which it does periodically and substantially — the most volatile series published here. UNITS: these are events, not people; one worker hired three times is three hires. Summing counties also counts a Summit-to-Stark move as one separation AND one hire, so the regional figure is inflated relative to any single-county comparison by an amount QWI cannot measure. Never write 'people'. FOOTPRINT: these are the 12 PIC-12 counties only. An earlier version published 139,180/137,727 because the derivation summed every row in qwi.json, which deliberately holds BOTH footprints — so the total was a 14-county mixture labeled PIC-12.

claims.assert: sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) == 168
claims.actual: sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])
claims.falsified_if: Any QWI revision. This is a flow-derived net, NOT the change in the employment stock — the stock reads 18,444 at the start and 17,725 at the end, and the page says so beside the chart.

claims.text: The beginning-of-quarter count reads 18,444 in 2012Q1 against 17,725 in 2025Q3, so the flow ledger is not the change in the stock.
claims.source: Census QWI Emp, first and last published quarters
claims.assert: D['quarters'][0]['emp'] == 18444 and D['quarters'][-1]['emp'] == 17725 and abs((D['quarters'][-1]['emp'] - D['quarters'][0]['emp']) - (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']))) > 500
claims.actual: (D['quarters'][0]['emp'], D['quarters'][-1]['emp'], sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']))
claims.falsified_if: A QWI revision that reconciles the seasonally adjusted stock with the seasonally adjusted flows. If the two ever agree within 500 jobs, the sentence in the flow chart's source line about them being estimated separately has to be rewritten, not just re-rounded.

claims.text: 55 quarters are drawn; the unpublished quarter is dropped, not zeroed.
claims.assert: len(D['quarters']) == 55 and all(q['counties'] > 0 for q in D['quarters'])
claims.falsified_if: QWI publishes 2025Q4 and the pipeline is not re-run.

claims.text: This page uses the PIC-12 footprint.
claims.falsified_if: FOOTPRINT: this page uses PIC-12, matching the cluster-health dashboard. It does NOT reconcile with the vault-sourced pages, which use NEO-14 — the two share only 10 counties.

claims.text: Every quarter covers all twelve PIC-12 counties.
claims.source: derive_rest.py filters qwi.json to the footprint and asserts full coverage
claims.assert: all(q['counties'] == 12 for q in D['quarters']) and len(D['meta']['footprint']['counties']) == 12
claims.falsified_if: Any quarter covers fewer than twelve counties — either QWI withheld one, or the pull is short and fetch_footprint.py needs re-running. This claim exists because the page published a 14-county total under a PIC-12 banner for weeks; a footprint that is merely STATED is not a footprint that is CHECKED. The flow chart's source line says 'no bar here is a floor' on the strength of this assertion, so if it fails that sentence is wrong too.

claims.text: About two thousand jobs start and about two thousand end in an average quarter.
claims.assert: round(sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) / 100) == 20 and round(sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) / 100) == 20
claims.actual: (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']), sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']))
claims.falsified_if: Either average leaves the 1,950-2,050 band, at which point 'about two thousand' in the flow chart's title stops being a fair rounding and has to be restated.

claims.text: The average quarter moves 10.8% of the workforce in or out.
claims.source: derived: mean of the 55 quarterly churn rates
claims.assert: round(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 100, 1) == 10.8
claims.actual: sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 100
claims.falsified_if: The mean moves off 10.75-10.85. This one figure carries the hero stat card, the shop-floor vignette and the translator's default sentence, so a tenth of a point moves three surfaces at once. UNITS: churn is the average of hires and separations over jobs, so 10.8% is 10.8% hired AND 10.8% separated, not 10.8% total movement.

claims.text: The four-quarter average reads 8.5% through 2012Q4 and 9.6% through 2025Q3, about 1.1 points higher.
claims.source: derived: trailing four-quarter means of the quarterly churn rate
claims.assert: round(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4 * 100, 1) == 8.5 and round(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 * 100, 1) == 9.6 and round((sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 1.1
claims.actual: (sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4 * 100, sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 * 100)
claims.falsified_if: Any of the three numbers shifts by a tenth of a point. The dashed reference line, the bracket label on the rate chart and the section's fig-title all print these, and QWI revisions of this size are ordinary — which is exactly why the note beside the chart calls the gap an estimate rather than a settled number.

claims.text: The four-quarter average has sat above its 2012 level in 51 of the 52 quarters it covers.
claims.source: derived: trailing four-quarter mean against the 2012 four-quarter mean
claims.assert: len(D['quarters']) - 3 == 52 and sum(1 for i in range(3, len(D['quarters'])) if sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4 > sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) == 51
claims.actual: sum(1 for i in range(3, len(D['quarters'])) if sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4 > sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4)
claims.falsified_if: The count drops below 48. This is the claim the revision note leans on: the endpoint gap could be revised away, but a revision would have to reverse the whole shape to take this with it. If the count falls, the note overstates its case.

claims.text: The four-quarter average peaked at 16.7% in 2022Q2.
claims.assert: D['quarters'][41]['year'] == 2022 and D['quarters'][41]['q'] == 2 and round(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][38:42]) / 4 * 100, 1) == 16.7 and close(max(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4 for i in range(3, len(D['quarters']))), sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][38:42]) / 4, 1e-12)
claims.actual: max((sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4, D['quarters'][i]['year'], D['quarters'][i]['q']) for i in range(3, len(D['quarters'])))
claims.falsified_if: The maximum lands in another quarter or off 16.65-16.75. The peak is labeled on the chart by value and by year, so a shift breaks both.

claims.text: Hiring bottomed at 1,373 in 2020Q2 and peaked at 4,106 in 2022Q1.
claims.assert: min(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) == 1373 and max(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) == 4106 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['year'] == 2020 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['q'] == 2 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 4106)['year'] == 2022 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 4106)['q'] == 1 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['seps'] == 1872

claims.assert: round((sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 1.9 and round((sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 0.2 and round((sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 0.9
claims.actual: ((sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, (sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100)
claims.falsified_if: Either component moves by a tenth of a point, or the two stop summing to twice the headline churn gap. This is the page's third act: if the hire-side rise turns out to be the larger one, the section title, the lede and the chart all assert the opposite of the data. IDENTIFICATION: this is a decomposition of an identity, not an explanation — nothing here says why people are leaving.

claims.text: On a four-quarter average, separations have run above hires in each of the eleven quarters since 2023Q1.
claims.source: derived: separation rate minus hire rate, trailing four quarters
claims.assert: D['quarters'][44]['year'] == 2023 and D['quarters'][44]['q'] == 1 and all(sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) > sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) for i in range(44, len(D['quarters']))) and sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][40:44]) < sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][40:44]) and len(D['quarters']) - 44 == 11

claims.text: County rates run from 6.2% in Mahoning to 13.5% in Trumbull, and nine of the twelve recorded more separations than hires.

SMALL NUMBERS: Trumbull's rate rests on 402 jobs, so it is the cell most likely to move on revision and the one the chart annotates as 'high rate, small base'. The default verdict sentence under the county selector prints all three numbers.

claims.text: At a 150-person plant, 10.8% quarterly churn is about sixteen hires and sixteen departures a quarter, five of each in a month, and about 65 replacement hires a year.
claims.source: derived: the mean quarterly churn rate applied to a 150-person payroll
claims.assert: round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters'])) == 16 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) / 3) == 5 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 4) == 65 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 * 4) == 58
claims.actual: (150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']), 150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 4)
claims.falsified_if: Any of the four numbers moves by one. This guards the translator's DEFAULT state, which is the 150-person case printed in the section lede and in the widget before anything is typed; other headcounts are the same arithmetic and are unguarded by design. ILLUSTRATIVE: it applies a cluster average to a single site and is not a measurement of any plant.

claims.text: The region started 6.0 times its own opening workforce, and the 222,890 hire and separation events are about 1,327 times the net.
claims.source: derived: total hires over opening employment; total events over net
claims.assert: round(sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / D['quarters'][0]['emp'], 1) == 6.0 and sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) == 222890 and round((sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])) / (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']))) == 1327
claims.actual: (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / D['quarters'][0]['emp'], (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])) / (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])))
claims.falsified_if: The multiple leaves 5.95-6.05 or the ratio leaves 1,322-1,332. The ratio is unstable by construction: its denominator is a small difference of two large numbers, so a revision of a few hundred events moves it by hundreds. That fragility is the reason the closer says 'about'.
